Credits

Journalist and broadcaster Michael Fitzpatrick has run with all the big game of journalism while inhabiting more countries than is absolutely necessary.

TOKYO —Nothing triggers the bog-walloping Fenian in me quite like a visit to the British Embassy. This one, with its fine Georgian-revival facade, looked on my last visit a decade ago like a lost Cotswold manor-house brought to life in Tokyo.

But what was it that I found so unsettling? Perhaps the stately setting? Or its gilt-framed displays of a preternaturally regal, late queen? Her gaze following me about the room as I moved among the fine art and mahogany, like those creepy Sacred Heart of Jesus portraits I grew up with. Me, a lad reared in an Irish republican home where the Queen’s annual Christmas messages were as welcome as a poltergeist.

To the more clubbable, the embassy’s English country house manner would have seemed merely civilized; a demonstration that Merrie England had acquired over generations the ability to arrange the upholstery without the aid of an AI shepherd.

The decor was a projection of centuries of British self-assuredness and ease, distilling, as adroitly as the form allows, the essence of (an ebbing) sovereign power. The fine art, damask and agreeable lighting gave no hint that Britain’s technological might has long migrated elsewhere. That such hegemony now lies with American platforms and Asian supply chains. But the genius of spaces like these is that you can start to believe in a type of fanciful continuity of the imperishable.

It inveigles you into sharing a fantasy. This one being that if these old arrangements had survived war, decolonization, Tamagotchis and the mobile phone, perhaps it might survive the latest digital convulsions, too. Here was a refuge, some autonomy even, from the technological superpowers that increasingly own us. Proof that small jurisdictions of taste, privacy and human-scale abound.

Of course, like any contemporary state, the British must put on a show of modernity. Outside the embassy hung long banners declaring that England was now a “Unicorn Kingdom.” But from where I was standing, the oak heart of this very British establishment demurred. They had seen it all before. But it was co-opting some of Silicon Valley’s grandiose illusions just to be safe. Inside the older, more [powerful unicorns](https://www.press.jhu.edu/journals/lion-and-unicorn) of mythology resided sinewy on the royal coat of arms. Not just representing rarity, but purity and extreme ferocity, reminding me of some English public-schoolboys I knew.

But this is the great charm of the embassy interior — its refusal to update. Even in the face of economic realities and the dark, immutable forces that forge them. Here was a stand for the moral and institutional habits of our ancestors.

## **A Sinking Feeling**

Big Tech oligarchs can threaten to transform all that is before them, but the timeless endurance of this lived-in aristocratic grandeur will survive, I was starting to feel. Now I — sinking in someone else’s club chair — was beginning to get it.

Assailed by crypto pirates, the succubi of VC-led extractor corporatism and the [crumbling of knowledge work](https://www.noemamag.com/why-is-everyone-in-tech-so-sad/), we feel profoundly the foundations of power shifting ominously beneath us. Countering that are the Embassy’s older, time-tested values and their comforting familiarity. People like the faddish Steve Jobs would [probably](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Steve-Jobs/Walter-Isaacson/9781982176860) have hated it. Like death for Californians, he thought furniture was optional.

Beyond the embassy precincts, Japan too was stealing itself from Darwinian upheaval, slouching toward it from across the Pacific. That was 10 years ago. Now the evolution has landed, proposing a [shotgun wedding](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/us-tell-partners-they-must-pick-sides-ai-race-with-china-2026-08-14) with a prenuptial dubbed Pax Silica.

The vow is simple: Join _our_ techno view of the world or be made irrelevant by it.

Or you can do what the embassy valiantly attempts: indulge in wishful thinking that we are beholden to no one; sovereign power is unassailable and will prevail over any forces that seek to unseat it. Look! We have brass sconces! Damask pelmets!

Eventually, I allowed myself to be consoled, finding one of the ambassador’s snugglers, an oversized armchair, to sink into and reflect. Besides, despite residues of unease, it was too late to bolt. The mayor of London, Boris Johnson at the time, had been promised forth — attended by the nation’s press and its tech somebodies — to expand on a subject without any obvious tripwire: London’s thrusting home-grown cashless tech.

I had a fancy I might know better. As a former hack himself, Johnson knew how to give good copy, and I had an uncharitable thought he would not disappoint.

After all, Johnson had already just [snot-o-grammed](https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-london-34537841) a schoolboy in a game of mock rugby the day before. Metaphors for the bumbling, bruiser foreigner riding roughshod over finer Japanese sensibilities came tumbling off the press. And why not? We in the geographical West have plenty of form here.

> “Japan too was stealing itself from Darwinian upheaval, slouching toward it from across the Pacific. That was 10 years ago.”

Polite rebuffs, coded rebukes, and death threats from Japan aimed at preventing Johnny Foreigner from putting his size-12 welly through the shoji doors have often proved futile over the centuries. We were never much good at taking the hint.

It fell to U.S. Navy Commodore Matthew C. Perry in 1853 to finally dash aside Japan’s isolationist polite “Please Do Not Disturb” sign to demand, with menaces, access rights. [Included](https://dchenlin.pages.iu.edu/h207_2002/perry.htm) in the list of “diplomatic” offerings was a white flag, should the Japanese ever feel the need to employ it.

Almost touchingly British, this American politely tapping on the door while carrying a battering ram. And echoing today’s political realities, when faced with “having no cards,” capitulation must follow as night follows day.

## **Can’t Put A Good Man Down**

Now we had a capering politician on a trade mission to Japan for whom such blundering was just a warm-up act. Japan’s wall of unassailable, face-saving etiquette would ensure his next gaffe.

Johnson was on his pins, grandly pitching the City Boys’ latest Fintech triumph — its “light-years ahead” magical, cashless payments tech. The marvelous BRITISH tech in question was contactless IC (integrated circuit) cards, which made paying for travel on the tube absolute duck soup.

Pausing to ask rhetorically, “Who else can boast that?” he practically invited an intervention. And so … apostle of truth that I am, I did not hold back. From the press seats, I pointed out that Japanese travelers were largely already there should they wish it. Japan had had the cashless tech for years, and practically single-handedly conjured up the tech in question while others fumbled for dimes. A couple of years back, I had even completed a journey — with mixed results, I have to say — around Japan to try out humanity’s first tentative steps toward going cashless.

Obviously, no news of this had reached the British capital, or the ears of the mayor’s flunkies, because suddenly Johnson looked all in, spluttering into his cuffs: “Really, is this true!?” A sea of dark heads bobbed in assent.

“Have I just undermined the whole raison d’être of this event? So, what is my raison d’être for being here?” he queried, eyeing his aides. “Why was I not told this?”

Summing up the possibilities, I arrived at a few rapid deductions. Firstly, his immediate staff and the embassy had signally failed to do their homework. Secondly, too many of his hosts were equally bereft of the facts concerning their own country’s digital prowess in this matter.

Third, and most crucially, a naked emperor, no matter how richly deserving of exposure, is still an Emperor in Japan; only on pain of social death should he be confronted with the humiliating truth.

It was an object lesson in the terrifying extremes to which Japan is willing to take its impeccable manners. Selling coals to Newcastle may be ill-advised, but apparently in Japan the correct form is for Newcastle to politely deny the existence of its coal pits in the face of such magnificent British magnanimity.

Yet this gaffe can be forgiven, if only because the Japanese themselves were largely in the dark about their own tech — having long refused to trust anything but hard cash. Because of this typical national recalcitrance, the contactless technology perfected in Japan decades ago initially [went nowhere](https://www.mitsue.co.jp/english/global_ux/blog/201801/19_1400.html), no matter how hard any Japanese Boris Johnsons tried to push it. It was only after the tech took off in Europe and elsewhere in the 2000s that it gained a widespread local following.

## **The Root Of All Evil Is Progress**

For me, this became a quiet symbol of the failure of progress and of our rightful reluctance to submit unconditionally to its tyranny. A new tyranny that demands societies adapt to every new technology. But as Japan proved, we do not have to. The fact that Japanese innovation remained so entirely invisible, even to the fintech envoys themselves, is also symptomatic of how Japan’s tech research routinely fails to achieve a global impact commensurate with its genius.

What is missing, as is so often the case in Japan, is the aggressive cultural machinery required to turn raw research into a bankable international asset.

The country lacks, above all, the cultural instinct to shout its name from the rooftops. When advised to do so, heads are patiently shaken in agreement, and eventually, it’s determined that no shoestring is too threadbare for the task. Even the most prestigious startup factory at Tokyo University has only one part-time PR rep. She does not speak English.

> “What is missing, as is so often the case in Japan, is the aggressive cultural machinery required to turn raw research into a bankable international asset.”

Consequently, there is very little understanding of how global visibility is created.

Treating communications, international business development and storytelling as peripheral administrative functions suggests a genuine contradiction here. Universities are being ordered to create globally competitive companies but seem blind to the fact that they are institutionally unsuited for the task. After observing such behavior time and time again in Japan, the communications gap is glaringly real.

Could such attitudes be an atavistic return to the days when storytellers, entertainers and the like were [classified](https://hilo.hawaii.edu/campuscenter/hohonu/volumes/documents/NotEvenHumanTheBirthoftheOutcasteinTokugawaJapan.pdf) under Japan’s feudal caste system as literally “[hinin](https://www.pbs.org/empires/japan/resources_4.html)” non-humans?

A suspicion, not unwarranted, that marketing and PR, like all stories, are a kind of … lies. Manipulative ones at that. When I asked about the story from these cloistered university startup hubs, the basic reply was, “Anyway, what use is a mere ‘story’ when you have specs!?”

Was this where Japan was failing startup-wise? I wondered.

## **Never Losing The Plod**

A few years later, I think I heard my answer: “It’s not about the tech, it’s about the execution,” explained one Tokyo tech insider at a startup meeting.

Where Japan often fails, he continued, was the slow pace of business. He was right. Japanese commerce likes to plod, and the Japanese are inveterate plodders. Decisions take months, even years, to kick things around, assess, assess, assess, then slowly “build trust” for the sake of “nemawashi” (preparations).

Japan’s sluggish adoption of cashless payments perfectly illustrated this trend. What was lost on its hapless Japanese inventors and investors was that they alone held the keys and were the legislators and instigators of a powerful new digital tool that the Tech Tyrants across the ocean had failed to monopolize.

Londoners, forever with an eye out for every angle, understood better. Fintech of this ilk being perhaps its only success yet at stemming a tide of American tech dominance, there was much to harumph about. While not a wholly British success story, it was about the only Big Tech triumph the UK could cling to before burlier Fin-Tech Bros sharp-elbowed them back to their country estates.

In the face of it, Japan and the UK seem powerless to stop this leaking away of sovereignty. Japan’s puzzling foot-dragging on the tech illustrates an overlooked aspect of its innovation drive — its long history of brilliant innovations that were, for various reasons, overlooked and sidetracked. It also illustrates very well Japan’s institutional-character problem and its uncanny ability to turn wine into water.

## **Opportunity Knocks**

It was Toyota that ushered me into one of its first commercial electric cars 30 years ago. Ditto, a self-driving vehicle that same year. Thanks to a “mad-scientist dream” for humanoid robots, a Japanese computer scientist told me 15 years ago that her country led the world in AI machine learning. Now, like Japan’s version of the Rip Van Winkle tale, Taro Urashima, the nation is waking up to find it overslept in all these fields.

Its less cautious neighbors, famously, ran with the tech Japan had been quietly pioneering, leaving the country on the wrong side of a technological divide entirely of its own making. The American giants, meanwhile, rose rapidly, ate everyone else’s lunch, pocketed their dinner money and now appear to be talking options on any future breathing plans others may be foolishly having.

That’s why we rant about Amazon, Apple, Meta, and the like as tech’s “Magnificent Seven,” and not the Seven Samurai. Contemporary Japan simply often fails to capitalize on, or communicate, its genius.

China, too, is leaving Japan and the rest of us at the bedroom door. It may have gotten its lead by “distilling” all the best ideas from Japan and elsewhere, but China is now outpacing us with the speed it has put these applications to use.

Ask any savvy Japanese, “How so?” and they’ll evoke the “Galápagos” theory. Like the plants and creatures on those famous islands, Japan’s tech standards and business practices have developed a unique character incompatible with overseas wants and desires.

Even the country’s myriad startups throw up lots of weird and wonderful concepts only seen in Japan, earning them domestic fans but a condemned death march if tempted to ship abroad due to their lack of marketing savvy and other entrepreneurial qualities. Because to grow globally, Japan lacks the linguistic skills, overengineers its products and fails to understand what might play well abroad. Nor is it an accident that Japanese researchers boast the most recipients of the Ig Nobel prizes, an annual satirical [award](https://fortune.com/2012/09/20/panda-dung-robot-undergrads-and-the-worlds-wackiest-tech-awards/) presented by the “Annals of Improbable Research” science humor magazine.

> “Japan’s puzzling foot-dragging on the tech illustrates an overlooked aspect of its innovation drive — its long history of brilliant innovations that were, for various reasons, overlooked and sidetracked.”

## **A New Kind Of Innovation**

There was even a craze called Chindōgu for what became known as useless “curious or strange tools,” in the ‘80s and ‘90s when Japan actually made stuff the world wanted.

This Galápagosian inward focus, while fostering some unique innovations, has also left Japan isolated in the global tech landscape, or so the thinking goes. This created a superficially hi-tech Japan, Hideki Onda, a former Apple director, once told me.

Onda believed Japan’s deeply cautious and conservative business and political classes were the root cause. This allowed Japan to evolve along Galápagos lines because the ruthless nature of startup capitalism and radical technocratic disruption was such a poor fit for Japan’s slower, more considered way of doing things.

When economists were chivying for the re-ignition of Japan’s competitive “animal spirits,” the country responded with its trademark animal caution.

To best illustrate this, Onda recalled a time in 1996 when Apple was pushing Japan to introduce its teaching tech to schools. The education minister’s answer was a polite “Kekko desu,” or no.

Apple’s then-CEO Michael Spindler asked Onda when they might return to try again. “When the ‘60s-era floor indicator above the ministry’s elevator door goes digital,” Onda told him.

A decisively Luddite response, many thought at the time. But fast-forward through 30 years of digitization, and we are seeing method in the minister’s madness. The rush to digitization and the digital economy, we found belatedly, has resulted in its own [casualties](https://www.noemamag.com/the-last-days-of-social-media/%5d).

The American models of capital efficiency and market disruption we so admired are now being seen as possibly ruinous. We are learning, for one, that networked screen-based learning is no silver bullet. Nor do all cultures suit the startup models; just ask the equal-with-Japan on social-cohesion-first Swedes.

## **The Medium Is The Message**

After noting a drop in student literacy, Sweden has now reversed its push toward digital learning. Cellphones have been banned in schools, and the textbook industry rejoices at schools’ return to paper.

And yet the assault from a proselytizing Big Tech on Japan, where digitization has been slow and AI remains largely a curiosity in the workplace, is intensifying.

There is still an unfulfilled desire to digitize; that is true. Broadcast mainly from some business quarters and certain politicos. Japan’s AI regulations, for instance, have been made as loose as those in the U.S., and many see them as an incentive for American corporations to move in.

I asked a Japanese friend and tech journalist what he thought about this new “Black Ships” moment, and he told me he expects an awkward culture clash of Titanic proportions. “Because American technology companies are often extraordinarily irresponsible about the social consequences of what they build.”

He had another keen observation for me: “Ultimately, Silicon Valley is not primarily optimized to maximize human wellbeing. It is optimized to maximize returns.”

Japan. Ostensibly capitalistic, has a rather different take. The [emphasis](https://www5.cao.go.jp/zenbun/wp-e/wp-je06/06-00202.html) is on social cohesion, not profits. This contrast is not simply cultural. In a 2006 Japanese government survey, nearly 70% of responding Japanese companies said employees were important stakeholders, and 90% planned to maintain long-term employment.

He now suspects that when we look back several decades, or perhaps several centuries, from now, we may conclude that our current tech revolution produces too much “technological pollution” — innovations that ultimately caused considerable suffering to large numbers of people despite Silicon Valley’s innovative bent. This is particularly daunting in light of well-informed concerns that AI development will lead to our extinction.

His conclusion echoes Japan’s nascent clarion call for “technological sovereignty.” It is now the responsibility, not of America, but of countries with long histories and deep cultural traditions such as in Europe, Japan and elsewhere, to propose ways of using technology that engage much more seriously with social responsibility, he argues.

And it is true that some Europeans and Japanese are now working to reduce their dependency on U.S. tech. But when you don’t have the cards, a certain raspy voice likes to remind us, the white flag your pushy competitors hand you can seem like a lifesaver after all.

## **Techno Darwinism Dawns**

Until the triumph of such heretics, the inescapable dark logic of techno Darwinism gets to cast its shade far into Japan’s corridors of power for now. Supping with the Devil as a hedge against total irrelevance, you might want to call it. Just bring long chopsticks and hope you are not on the menu.

> “The rush to digitization and the digital economy, we found belatedly, has resulted in its own casualties.”

Presiding over national decline and a plummeting yen, Peter Thiel’s recent appearance in Tokyo must have seemed an omen of sorts to the government — perhaps even an opportunity. Certainly, Japan’s premier Sanae Takaichi received Thiel and his trade mission cheerfully enough, despite any whiff of sulfur. Besides being something of a missionary from the darker side of the Singularity faithful, his visit was the latest in a long list of tech emissaries from across the water. U.S. venture capital, too, is arriving fast. Marc Andreessen , boss of one of the heftiest firms, opened his first overseas office in Japan this summer. It is no secret that Japan [now sees](https://www.jetro.go.jp/en/invest/investment_environment/ijre/report2023/ch3/sec10.html) the Silicon Valley model as the one that might get it out of its considerable hole.

Brandon Hill, founder of an outfit that helps startups on both sides of the Pacific, told me Tokyo is desperate for more startups and more “successful exits.” The hope is that those eager entrepreneurs will spark another period of rapid reinvention like the 19th-century’s Meiji-era modernization, or Japan’s dramatic re-industrialization after World War II. This one, we imagine, will be driven by homegrown Silicon-Valley wannabes with less perishable wings of wax.

But Japan should be thinking beyond simply creating more startups, Hill insists, keen to impart to an attentive Japan the magic formula: “It should be creating more globally competitive companies.”

## **Death March, What Death March?**

But these are death march orders again. Because given Japan’s current climate of anxiety and its lack of survival skills, English and narrative nous, the global market will exact its toll. Once a nation of outward-looking, inveterate tinkerers willing to make technology central to national survival, the collapse of the ‘80s economic boom in 1991 led to lost decades and economic stagnation. The bust also created a fear of risk-taking and a retreat into safe jobs, safe investments and safe conservative governments.

Thanks to that trauma, contemporary Japan is a much more inward-looking and risk-averse place now. The bubble’s collapse and the financial crisis that followed gave way to a long corporate decline. In a 2024 [survey](https://www.boj.or.jp/en/research/brp/rer/rerb240628.htm), the Bank of Japan found that many firms had curbed investment and built cash reserves after the crisis and later shocks. That history helps explain business caution, though it cannot by itself explain Japan’s wider inward turn.

The moral and institutional habits formed by Japan’s lost decades are unlikely to evaporate at the urging of a few Tech Valley gurus. Many here, perhaps rightly, take pride that the Libertarian, go-getting style of the buccaneering new world capitalists remains as rare as buttered sushi.

Despite this, some sections of central government, such as the bullish Ministry of Economy, are insisting the nation pledges its shirt to such a miraculous resurrection of entrepreneurial spirits. Even if it means the much-dreaded importing — however imperfectly — of alien business practices, plus accommodating the Devil of foreign investment and all its stratagems.

The current thinking is, if Japan’s satraps are to become Satan’s latest freshly minted imps so that the country can flourish, so be it. Accordingly, Japan’s ministries must undergo a Damascene conversion, buckle under for universal digitization, get with the program and ditch the fax for the splendid shining lie of the startup. Strong medicine for a nation that swears by “not waking the baby.”

## **The Revolution Will Not Be Commodified**

As already mentioned, the revolution will not be restricted to business. Shanghaied into the program are its universities, too, to be raided for startup recruits. They now giddily employ the magic word salads of “incubators,” “ecosystems” and “unicorns” — incantations in the newly imported, and hopefully profitable, cargo cult.

In service to the “Stack” — the secret sauce of the vaunted digital product — they must dump the Old-Fogey seats of learning/babysitting roles and learn to “hyper-scale.” And in doing so, become the engines of a “new technology-driven nation” where science and technology provide economic growth and national security. The model is California’s lucrative fusion of pioneering lab work and entrepreneurship stripped for export.

This is a big ask for an institution whose principal role, until now, was an untaxing refuge for students lately overtaxed by Japan’s notorious entrance exams.

But the heart wants what the heart wants. So out must go the playground-cum-finishing school model applied to the young before they join the workforce. It is a system that makes them easy targets for job automation anyway.

> “The moral and institutional habits formed by Japan’s lost decades are unlikely to evaporate at the urging of a few Tech Valley gurus.”

Research at the top universities is another matter entirely. World-class and innovative but sheltered from the worldly West Coast-style monetizing of know-how, they are an unlikely vehicle for commerce. But to the trendier, more tech-savvy of Tokyo’s mandarins, gifting academic researchers with money and startup blueprints must seem like a foolproof remedy for Japan’s economic woes.

The country’s economic emergency is real enough. Japan’s nominal GDP, which once ranked second in the world, fell to third place in 2010 and then to fourth place in 2023. The country’s share of global nominal GDP has fallen sharply, from approximately 18% in 1995 to approximately 3.8% in 2025. More worryingly, its nominal GDP per capita has [also fallen](https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/cr/2026/english/1jpnea2026001.pdf) from second in the world to 38th today.

Real wages have stagnated for 30 years; the yen has fallen to a low not seen for nearly 40 years.

## **Ingredients But No Recipe**

But there are reasons for hope. After all, the country has all the ingredients to make it a supreme techno-state. Elite scientists, a magic-money spigot (take a bow, quantitative easing and near-zero interest rates) and world-class manufacturing chops.

But instead of impacting our world with its surprisingly useful research applications, the policies, as my tech writer friend pointed out, are only exposing an almighty clash of civilizations. It’s another institutional mismatch where Japanese universities, slow and hierarchical to their bones, repurpose poorly as startup factory incubators (which must be fast and unstable). The friction is almost palpable.

After decades of being left to their own insular devices — including, bizarrely, a reluctance to publish abroad — university-linked founders are now lining up to take grants for “global startups” while conveniently skipping the global part. No slogan has ever been emptier than “be global from the start,” as [most of these](https://beyondnextventures.com/jp/insight/brave2023-demoday-healthtech?) founders [don’t speak English](https://x.com/taishiyade/status/2092153788845187457?s=20).

But without the “[go global](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/norbertgehrke_jic-going-global-status-of-japanese-startups-ugcPost-7335518927050940416-3O2T/)!” declaration, they would be unlikely to qualify for funding. This makes Japan’s latest bid to race across borders, like all its other vaunted internationalization schemes, a sham.

Because Japan lingers in the [bottom ranks](https://www.ef.com/wwen/epi) of English proficiency tests and belatedly adopts international marketing practices, like pitching or self-promotion, its innovation remains mostly invisible to a broader public.

Without a sudden sea-change, conjuring national self-reliance, economic security and cutting-edge innovation out of Japan’s unbelievably stuffy, risk-averse and archaic institutions will be a miracle. Already, in critical fields like AI, semiconductors and defense tech, the chance to lead sailed away with the last of the country’s frustrated emigre innovators.

## **Enter The Zombies**

But appealing fictions have a habit of overriding the stark facts. So universities take a [substantial amount](https://www.jst.go.jp/program/startupkikin/files/sogyo/2025koubosetumei_sogyo.pdf) of government money to pump out startups despite being poorly equipped to produce global-ready startups as the state is requesting. Most of these universities focus on Japan’s stockpile of zombie enterprises — the kinds that have stayed alive thanks to cheap credit and government handouts rather than healthy, global market performance.

Japanese startups outside the blessed and coddled circle of academia fare no better. Lacking the swagger of Silicon Valley, Japan’s corporate culture is the antithesis of America’s individualistic, T-shirted tycoons. Japan’s corporate culture prioritizes conformist don’t-rock-the-boat mediocrity, uses generalists rather than specialists, and favors risk-aversion over disruptive ideas; monetizing innovation will remain a struggle. The Economist [suggests](https://www.economist.com/business/2026/08/13/japans-downbeat-startups-need-a-lift) Tokyo’s “startups first” growth plan looks woefully misguided.

Not that the country lacks the kind of Promethean chutzpah that could bring new light, energy and progress. But Japan has a habit of taking the role of an angry Zeus —chaining any unruly innovators to the nearest rock. Japan has a long list of disgruntled innovators who feel hard done by its corporate system. Even the chap who invented the white LED, [Shuji Nakamura](https://www.ibscdc.org/Case_Studies/Innovation%20and%20New%20Product%20Development/IPD0021.htm), was originally rewarded with a corporate bonus of just 20,000 yen (roughly $200 at the time).

## Scapegoat

If there is one man famous for bringing raw, individualistic U.S.-style techno-capitalism to these shores and failing spectacularly, it is [Takefumi Horie](https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2006-jun-06-fi-murakami6-story.html) — AKA “Horiemon.” No fire-bearing Titan to mankind is he — more an ambitious internet provider — but instructive all the same was the treatment of this tech startup founder imprisoned for 21 months for his disruptive antics a couple of decades ago.

Horie’s style put him at the center of a culture clash between U.S. and Japanese business. He became the scourge of Japanese companies when his internet firm Livedoor launched a hostile bid for Nippon Broadcasting in 2005. Using a legal loophole in off-hours trading, it bought 29.6% of the radio broadcaster in one go, bringing its holding to around a third. It was an attempt to take control of the powerful Fuji TV. The move led the government to change the Securities and Exchange law to extend takeover rules to off-hours trading. The bid failed.

> “Japan’s corporate culture prioritizes conformist don’t-rock-the-boat mediocrity, uses generalists rather than specialists, and favors risk-aversion over disruptive ideas; monetizing innovation will remain a struggle.”

Authorities arrested Horie a year later on a separate issue. He faced charges that his company Livedoor falsified financial results to mislead investors. The company reported a pretax profit of about 5 billion yen, but prosecutors said it had actually made a loss of about 300 million yen. Horie was convicted of securities-law violations and sentenced to 2 ½ years in prison, serving about 21 months.

Such treatment shocked Japan’s startup community and signaled that non-consensus-driven, Anglo-Saxon, morally ambiguous capitalism bent on erasing cultural norms might be tolerated in the U.S. but punished in Japan. Japanese tech startups aiming to be the tallest poppy at the time quickly pulled up their roots. The startup revolution and rush to digitization were canceled.

In the face of Japan’s bureaucratic top-down planning, Japan’s elite universities, patient capital and strong manufacturing record count for little. Fast-moving, software-driven global tech trends simply move on — too quickly for a Japanese catch-up.

This, despite Japan actually sharing the passion for tech America does. In the field of AI in particular, Japan’s affair with machine intelligence is relatively long and productive. Computer scientist [Noriko Arai](https://www.nytimes.com/2013/12/30/world/asia/computers-jump-to-the-head-of-the-class.html) sat me down in her office 15 years ago and explained how a “mad scientist” dream of humanoid robots placed Japan ahead in the AI race decades ago.

In the 1980s, while Western researchers were still skeptical of neural networks, Japanese scientists were diving deep into artificial neurons and machine learning. “We say Japan was ahead at the time,” AI researcher Yutaka Matsuo told me. “But perhaps that doesn’t mean a lot now.”

Japan fell behind, failing to catch the St. Vitus’s dance deemed necessary to animate a Silicon Valley-style digital resurrection. But perhaps we have been measuring the wrong thing. Yes, its institutions are often too conservative to change, but as we survey the damage that technology has inflicted upon us, were the plodders right to plod?

Fearlessness in the face of failure, rapid iteration, global self-confidence, impatience with hierarchy — are definitively not the country’s house style. But because of this, did Japan eventually dodge a bullet? My tech journalist friend and others like him increasingly feel so.

There are fears of a too-rapidly deployed foreign AI risk, fears over the erosion of social cohesion, fears that a gig economy will replace Japan’s cherished full employment. The call is also for more strategic autonomy from tech corporations who are outmaneuvering the locals.

## **Black Ships Redux**

But the chatter is not just of another Black Ships “coup” or “digital colonialism” if Japan adopts the American model of rapid disruption. There’s a growing realization that the friction of the culture clash is perhaps a benefit. Japan’s plodding ways and institutions incompatible with hyper-capitalism offer a chance to install some kind of rugged technological sovereignty. They allow Japan to escape the technological determinism now infecting the West.

The appearance of a technology doesn’t mean that societies are suddenly forced to adapt to it. Societies should decide which technologies to adopt, how quickly, under what rules and for whose benefit. In 2021, UNESCO called for human oversight and demanded that we give societies a basis to accept or reject AI systems. A call now responded to belatedly by institutions and governments worldwide, mirroring people’s concerns over AI developments.

Coincidentally, Johnson’s ill-timed Fintech speech I attended at the embassy shines a light on the assumption that every problem has a technological solution, and that more technology necessarily means progress. A technological determinism and the myth of technological progressiveness Japan should be keen to avoid.

“We have to recognize that disruptive technology is simply inevitable and we cannot put the technological genie back in the bottle,” Johnson added to his contactless payments pitch. “Once the toothpaste is out of the tube, folks, that’s it.”

## **Inertia Is Not All Bad News**

Do the Japanese need to become more Californian to be more capable, or should these old institutions and Japan’s inertia be left alone to create some breathing space? Bill Gates said recently there is “no plan to ease the entry into the AI era.” Perhaps Japan’s experience of friction at that very entry is telling us something. Despite its half-hearted attempts to mimic Silicon Valley values, the country’s deep inertia seems to be buffeting it from some of the ill effects of globalization and technological disruption.

For decades, Japanese companies have attempted to shield their workers from the insatiable demands of stockholders and capital as part of a “social responsibility” mindset to help create jobs and safeguard companies.

> “As outdated and sluggish as the nation’s institutions might be, their limbic caution has preserved livelihoods.”

As outdated and sluggish as the nation’s institutions might be, their limbic caution has preserved livelihoods. Because, as it has often been said, Japan is a massive job creation scheme. Any introduction of American-style lean capitalism would threaten the labor policies aimed at creating overemployment, and the men I see guiding traffic around roadworks outside my house where a traffic light would do would all be out of a job. Making Japan a possible, and unlikely, last stand to our current reckoning with technological determinism.

Everywhere else the old rules are breaking, and some are heading for the exit laden with unicorn silver. West Coast billionaires are even [reportedly](https://rushkoff.com/books/survival-of-the-richest.html) seeking escape hatches or bunkers. Could tardy Japan be on their list of hideaways?

Exchange Tokyo for Vienna in this old joke and you’ll see what I mean. “If the world should ever come to an end — move to Vienna, because everything there happens 20 years later,” goes the quip used even today about the celestial city.

Japan is not unlike Vienna in this respect in its refusal to update. And its failure to do so, like the unabashed, unreconstructed British Embassy in Tokyo, may not be a disadvantage at all. On the contrary, it can remind us of what we value, and why.

Intellectuals get great motivation from big grand questions, and often do work adjacent to them, intending to be relevant to them. Such intellectuals mostly get prestige for the observable impressive detail of their work. Detail such as data collection, stat analysis, game theory models, agent-based models, case studies, phil analysis, engaging public essays, compelling keynote talks, and managing related orgs.

When the world changes its mind on such questions, intellectuals who are sufficiently prestigious due to their details often gain even more prestige from the fact that they had supported those new positions in their work well before the world did. And such intellectuals like to credit their details for contributing to this intellectual progress.

However, intellectual opinions on big grand questions are usually driven more than they like to admit by simple abstract arguments, often processed intuitively. We usually form such opinions soon after hearing of such questions, and then may change our minds as new such arguments occur to us.

When forming opinions based on abstract arguments, and opaque intuitions, it is possible to be either sloppy and fast, or careful and slow. Yet it is hard to tell from the form of the results just how much work went into them. The space of abstract arguments is so vast that both approaches result in pretty simple-looking abstract arguments. As a result, it is hard to impress audiences with such arguments. Which is why prestige is given mostly for associated impressive detail.

The problem here is that even though abstract arguments are in fact typically relevant and potent for drawing conclusions regarding big grand questions, intellectuals spend most of their efforts on less potent adjacent details. If we would instead think harder on the abstract arguments, we’d plausibly make much faster intellectual progress.

Well-subsidized prediction markets re future intellectual opinions on big grand questions would be one way give stronger incentives to think harder about abstract arguments. But don’t expect the intellectuals now gaining prestige via their impressive details to offer much support for this change.

> The problem here is that even though abstract arguments are in fact typically relevant and potent for drawing conclusions regarding big grand questions, intellectuals spend most of their efforts on less potent adjacent details. If we would instead think harder on the abstract arguments, we’d plausibly make much faster intellectual progress.

Robin, I find it impossible to figure out how this assertion is supposed to map onto reality. When you say intellectuals spend most of their efforts, how do you propose to measure effort? I might propose the time spent writing, the word count, the budget, the time spent experimenting. I think any of those methods would show the overwhelming majority of effort being spent on details in any scientific endeavor. Science requires data, methodology, statistical models. The only kind of intellectual who spends more time on abstract ideas than on data, is a philosopher, or a humanities professor; and the quality of their work suffers terribly from that weakness.

To me, "think harder on the abstract arguments" sounds like you're telling intellectuals to write like Marxists or art critics. It sounds like you're recommending intellectuals /think/ top-down--that they start and end with abstractions. That sounds like rejecting the Enlightenment and turning from empiricism back to rationalism. And it sounds like math, which is respectable, but not a science, atypical, and probably not what you want to talk about.

Or, you're telling them to write like Malcolm Gladwell. Malcolm Gladwell picks one counter-intuitive heuristic, then piles up anecdote upon anecdote in which that heuristic worked. What he never, ever does is tell us how he chose his anecdotes, or how many anecdotes he threw out because they came out the wrong way, or look for some commonalities between the anecdotes where the heuristic worked , and commonalities between the anecdotes where it didn't. Gladwell lists enough details to make each anecdote complete, but doesn't /think/ about how the details affect whether the heuristic works.

I don't know what you mean when you ask "should we think more about the details or the abstraction?" Most good intellectual arguments are a pyramid, with a wide base of data at the bottom, and one abstract proposition at the top. If you're not telling the pyramid builder to gather more capstones than foundation stones, then what do you mean to say?

I understand intuitively that there is a balance to be struck here. Clearly some studies are too lost in abstractions (say, Hegel or Heidegger). But these are cases when the abstractions are not grounded in reality, or at least in a common non-metaphysical language (rather than the specialized, recursive, meaningless languages of Hegel and Heidegger). And some studies are trawls of data which end up being uninformative because not enough of the details of the various pieces of data have been worked out to get any use of of them, like the Human Genome Project. So, a project can over-emphasize either abstraction or details.

But if we want to talk meaningfully about balance, well, we're going to have to use math. We're going to have to specify a mathematical function relating the amount of attention given to each level of abstraction, as a function of its specificity. The "pyramid" model is linear, and says quantity(L) ~ specificity(L)^2. In most real-world examples of scientific problems, quantity(L) ~ c^specificity(L), where c is probably > 2, would be more realistic.

It might be interesting, but this doesn't strike me as a good methodology for getting accurate answers. The methodology that works for me is just to notice where the information gaps are in your model, and pay more attention to the parts you don't yet know enough about. No fussing about with idealized equations, which are rather like assuming a cow is a perfect sphere.

title: Skinner, Cattell, Stewart, Wilson on Deliberate Culture
content:
My analysis of cultural drift has (at least) three distinctive elements:

1.   We have a big problem: we broke our process for the evolution of (not in) cultures.

2.   Instead of reviving blind evolution, it might be better to evolve deliberately

3.   I have three concrete ideas for institutional mechanisms of deliberate evolution.

I asked an LLM for book authors who have also made my #2 point, on deliberate cultural evolution. It gave 4: Skinner (’71), Cattell (‘87), Stewart (’00), Wilson (’19). All seem to understand the nature of cultural evolution, all argue for our working harder to understand and think in terms of evolution, all say we might plausibly win in evolutionary terms if we were to more consciously manage cultural evolution, and all say to do this at least in part via governance.

However, none offer concrete mechanism solutions re how to induce governance leaders to effectively manage cultural evolution, instead of pretending to do so while actually serving themselves and their allies. I’m thinking that this might be my most unusual stance in this space, and so maybe what I should focus my writing there on.

The best book was the earliest: B.F. Skinner (’71) _Beyond Freedom and Dignity:_

> Many were offended by this and tried to rejected it by rejecting his behavioralism framework. But the arguments in his book are mostly independent of behavioralism. Skinner correctly notes that commitments to freedom and dignity might limit the wins of deliberate evolution. He gets that we’d need to design good institutions to keep controllers in line, but offers no ideas re how to do that.

The worse written book is: Raymond Cattell (’87) _Beyondism: Religion From Science:_

> He is the least focused on governance, does not at all want a world government, but does want pretty direct DNA eugenics, and wants a new supporting movement that takes on more of a religious character.

The least famous of the 3 authors is: John Stewart (’00) _Evolution’s Arrow:_

> Stewart insists that markets are not good enough, but also admits existing forms of governance are not good enough. We must both change out individual psychologies to value adaption, and also adopt much better governance forms. He gives the name “vertical markets” to a better form, but mainly just associates that name with many desirable features, without a concept of how they could be achieved.

The most recent is the most political: David Sloan Wilson (’19) _This View of Life_

> Wilson says economics and economists are terrible, everything needs regulation, and we must make a world government designed to max world welfare. He doesn’t clarify how that might square with max adaption. He admits the problem of world governance is hard, says not to use markets or central planning, and points to many particular small orgs he admires, including communes.

Here are many quotes from those books:

**BF Skinner (’71)**_**Beyond Freedom and Dignity:**_

The intentional design of a culture, with the implication that behaviour is to be controlled, is sometimes called ethically or morally wrong. …

CuIture[’s] … main effect … is to bring the individual under the control of the remoter consequences of his behaviour. The effect has had survival value in the process of cultural evolution, since practices evolve because those who practise them are as a result better off. …

[But] we say that there is something ‘morally wrong’ about a totalitarian state, a gambling enterprise, uncontrolled piecework wages, the sale of harmful drugs, or undue personal influence, not because of any absolute set of values, but because all these things have aversive consequences. …

The intentional design of a culture and the control of human behaviour it implies are essential if the human species is to continue to develop. …

Those who have been induced by their culture to act to further its survival through design must accept the fact that they are altering the conditions under which men live and, hence, engaging in the control of human behaviour. Good government is as much a matter of the control of human behaviour as bad. …

Our culture has produced the science and technology it needs to save itself. It has the wealth needed for effective action. It has, to a considerable extent, a concern for its own future. But if it continues to take freedom or dignity, rather than its own survival, as its principal value, then it is possible that some other culture will make a greater contribution to the future. …

Abstract thinking is the product of a particular kind of environment, not of a cognitive faculty. … The physical and biological technologies which have increased man’s sensitivity to the world around him and his power to change that world have taken no more than four or five generations. …

C. S. Lewis protested : ... ‘the power of man to make himself what he pleases means ... the power of some men to make other men what they please’. This is inevitable in the nature of cultural evolution. …

For a long time men have introduced new practices which serve as cultural mutations, and they have changed the conditions under which practices are selected. They may now begin to do both with a clearer eye to the consequences. …

The individualist … has refused to be concerned for the survival of his culture and is not reinforced by the fact that the culture will long survive him. In the defence of his own freedom and dignity he has denied the contributions of the past and must therefore relinquish all claim upon the future. Science has probably never demanded a more sweeping change in a traditional way of thinking about a subject, nor has there ever been a more important subject. …

Physical and biological technologies have alleviated pestilence and famine and many painful, dangerous, and exhausting features of daily life, and behavioural technology can begin to alleviate other kinds of ills. … There are wonderful possibilities - and all the more wonderful because traditional approaches have been so ineffective. It is hard to imagine a world in which people live together without quarrelling, maintain themselves by producing the food, shelter, and clothing they need, enjoy themselves and contribute to the enjoyment of others … Yet all this is possible. …

The designer of a culture comes under fire because explicit design implies control (if only the control exerted by the designer). The issue is often formulated by asking : Who is to control? And the question is usually raised as if the answer were necessarily threatening. To prevent the misuse of controlling power, however, we must look not at the controller himself but at the contingencies under which he engages in control. … The great problem is to arrange effective counter-control and hence to bring some important consequences to bear on the behaviour of the controller.

**Raymond Cattell (’87)**_**Beyondism: Religion From Science**_

Evolution is the prime process visible in the universe, to which we have to conform, and should do so in good will. … Human evolution proceeds by ultimately by evolution in groups. … Natural selection among groups and individuals requires … adequate variation. …. The evolution of the best inter-individual ethical values is therefore based finally on the processes of intergroup differential survival. …

The spiritual life of Beyondism arises, in part, like that of the other religions, from genetic urges unsatisfied in everyday life, unavoidably in any culture with genetic lag. Beyondism differs in shaping those desires explicitly to logically indicated evolutionary needs.

There are six main entities to which an individual’s ethical values can be functionally oriented: fellow group members, the group government, other group governments, members of other groups, individuals committed to a Beyondist Ethic, and above all the Evolutionary Purpose.

Culture changes bye the mechanical and social inventions of leading persons, and by borrowing (willing or forced) from other cultures.

Culture as a whole is likely to demand more complete adjustments from the general population than they are suited to make. This discrepancy we call genetic lag. … is the cause of many social problems,

Beyondism … concludes first that a substantial freedom for individuality is required. … When ethical rules are scientifically derived from social research, egoistic, antisocial individualism can be treated in distinction from creative individualism.

Beyondism calls practically for a vast increase in social research, with such objectives as making national comparisons, defining ethical systems, clarifying the ethical and cultural values of each group, and so on. For each group should follow its own divergent adventures, racially and culturally, in cooperative competition with a world federation of groups, each with its own sociobiological research institutes.

If survival is the final test of ethics, our ethical values, and the political practices resulting, need serious re-education … and the acceptance of direction by qualified elites, democratically watched.

A positive eugenic condition could be most simply established by an ethic of more children from the socially more successful. The mechanics would require some economic laws.

**David Sloan Wilson (’19)**_**This View of Life**_

Compared to where we started ten thousand years ago, well-functioning governance at the scale of the whole earth seems just within reach. …

the modern economics profession rests upon a pre-Darwinian foundation. … If human groups are to function like organisms, then they need to be regulated … Labor unions became strong, the state played an active role in social welfare and industrial development, … But [then] … selfish interests and ideologies that justified individual and corporate greed as good for the whole group began to spread, leading to our decline in well-being and increase in political discord …

The whole cannot be optimized by separately optimizing the parts. That’s why the concept of the invisible hand in orthodox economic theory, which pretends that the pursuit of lower-level self-interest robustly benefits the common good, is so deeply flawed. …

The most important conclusion for our purposes is that cultural group selection must become more intentional and deliberative than ever before. … To solve problems at the planetary scale, we must formulate policies with the welfare of the whole planet in mind.

There is something between centralized planning and laissez-faire that can work: a managed process of variation and selection. First there must be a target that we are aiming to hit. For a business, this might be profitability, social responsibility, or the development of a new product line. At the planetary scale, it might be a robust global economy or the reduction of greenhouse gases. These targets become the criteria for selection, …

We can deliberately formulate alternative strategies for reaching the target goals, comparing them to each other and to current practices using rigorous statistical methods. …

I have provided three examples of adaptable societies. All of them are drawn from the business world,

economy. But decades are required and each cultural lineage comes against barriers that limit its distribution,

Clearly, more is needed for human groups of all sorts to adapt to change at the speed and scale that is required to solve the myriad problems of our age. … The first step is to adopt the right theory. … The right theory is based on the cultural evolution of complex systems. … Making our societies more adaptable won’t be easy, especially at larger scales, but it will be possible with the right blueprint provided here by evolutionary theory, multilevel selection, and a solid four-question approach.

Cultural transmission represents another mechanism of heredity in many species, one that has become vastly more powerful in humans with the advent of symbolic thought. … The bottom line for our purposes is that there is nothing wrong with the concept of conscious evolution. …

Once we become comfortable with the concept of conscious evolution, then the need to design our personal and cultural evolutionary processes becomes clear, similar to designing an evolutionary algorithm on a computer. This is what biologists call “the evolution of evolvability.” If we don’t become wise managers of evolutionary processes, then evolution will still take place but will lead to outcomes that are not aligned with our normative goals. …

If we want the whole earth to become a superorganism, then multilevel selection theory tells us exactly what to do: make planetary welfare the target of selection. This is easier said than done. …

An evolutionary worldview makes two contributions toward actually achieving a whole earth ethic, as opposed to just wanting it when in the right frame of mind. First, it provides strong scientific support for the need to make the welfare of the whole earth the target of selection in the formulation of policies, which in turn can orchestrate the formulation of policies for all lower-level units. At the same time, it removes scientific support for the main alternative narrative, which is that the unregulated pursuit of lower-level self-interest robustly benefits the common good. …

Policy formulation must be a conscious evolutionary process that first chooses the right target of selection, then monitors planned and unplanned variation, and then replicates best practices, realizing that implementation might be highly contextual. …

All of us are in a position to make things happen at some scale, if only in our own lives and our immediate surroundings. … A remarkable example, with lessons for all of us, is an ecovillage called Dancing Rabbit … I have conducted a survey of over a hundred intentional communities … They scored near the top on measures of satisfaction and meaning of life …

What if you are a politician, policy expert, CEO of a business, or board member … Avoid the temptation of centralized planning. You and your expert consultants are not smart enough to know how to improve the complex system that is under your care. You should implement the core design principles, which are fundamentally inclusive. You should also implement evolutionary processes that identify the right targets of selection, monitor planned and unplanned variation, and replicate best practices, knowing that their implementation will be highly sensitive to context. Everyone within the complex system under your care will need to take part, as in the examples of Toyota, the rapid results method, and innovation ecosystems that I recounted in chapter 9. You will have far more success, recognition, and personal fulfillment than you would pretending to be a Master of the Universe. Here is something else that everyone can do: learn more about the evolutionary worldview. …

“this view of life” is the wave of the future. The main question is how soon it will arrive and whether it will be in time to avert the potential disasters that confront us.
